question: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.

raiseTranscript.text: When a new engineer joined my pod, I paired with them for the first two weeks on our ticket triage process. I walked through our repo structure and created a simple checklist of common gotchas from my own first month.
What was the outcome?
They closed their first ticket in week three instead of the usual five weeks. They told me the checklist saved them from repeating my early mistakes.
How did you balance this with your own work?
I blocked two hours a day and flagged it in my standup so the team knew I was deliberately slowing down a bit.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Individual contributor on a small pod
Situation: New engineer joined; candidate created checklist from own experience and paired daily
Actions: Blocked time, shared repo walkthrough and gotchas
Outcome: New hire closed first ticket in 3 weeks vs typical 5; positive feedback received
Quote: "They told me the checklist saved them from repeating my early mistakes."
Follow-up: How did you balance this with your own work? -> Blocked two hours/day and surfaced in standup
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at junior level. The candidate treated onboarding as shared ownership rather than an extra task. They reused their own onboarding pain points to create a reusable checklist and protected time explicitly. The result was measurable against the team norm (3 weeks vs 5). They also surfaced the time trade-off in standup, showing awareness of team impact. Biggest strength: proactive reuse of personal experience to accelerate someone else without waiting to be asked.

lowerTranscript.text: I answered questions when the new person asked me. Mostly about where files were.
Not really, I was busy with my own tickets so I just responded when pinged.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Individual contributor
Situation: New teammate joined the team
Actions: Only answered questions when asked; focused on own work
Outcome: No measurable acceleration mentioned
Quote: "I was busy with my own tickets so I just responded when pinged."
Follow-up: Did you do anything proactively? -> No structured help
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at junior level. The candidate viewed helping as reactive only and prioritized personal output without trade-off discussion. No evidence of ownership over the new hire's ramp or attempt to reduce repeated questions. The story shows minimal investment and no learning applied from their own experience. Biggest gap: treats collaboration as interrupt-driven rather than intentional support.

raiseTranscript.text: A new hire joined across two teams I worked with. I built a lightweight onboarding doc covering our cross-team handoff process and ran a 90-minute walkthrough with both teams' leads.
What changed?
The new person started contributing to joint planning sessions in week four. Before that, cross-team tickets were stuck for weeks because no one knew the other side's constraints.
How did you get buy-in from the other team?
I shared the draft doc with their lead first and asked what was missing so it wasn't just my view.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Senior IC influencing two teams
Situation: New hire needed to ramp on cross-team handoffs
Actions: Created shared doc, ran joint walkthrough, incorporated feedback from other lead
Outcome: New hire in joint planning by week 4; reduced stuck cross-team tickets
Quote: "I shared the draft doc with their lead first and asked what was missing."
Follow-up: How did you get buy-in from the other team? -> Co-created the content
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at senior level. The candidate extended help beyond their immediate team and influenced without authority by involving the other lead early. The doc addressed a systemic friction point rather than just individual questions. Outcome shows earlier contribution to joint work. Biggest strength: turned a single onboarding into reusable cross-team infrastructure while still seeking input from stakeholders.

lowerTranscript.text: I helped the new senior on my team by reviewing their first PRs in detail.
Did this affect other teams they needed to work with?
Not really, I focused on our team's code style.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Senior IC
Situation: New senior joined the candidate's team
Actions: Detailed PR reviews focused on team code style
Outcome: No mention of cross-team impact or broader ramp
Quote: "I focused on our team's code style."
Follow-up: Did this affect other teams they needed to work with? -> No
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at senior level. The candidate stayed within team boundaries and did not address the cross-team context that a senior role requires. Help remained tactical (PR reviews) rather than enabling broader effectiveness. No evidence of influence or scaling the help. Biggest gap: limited scope to immediate team despite the level expectation of cross-team impact.

raiseTranscript.text: When two new managers joined my org, I created a 30-60-90 onboarding plan and paired each with a peer mentor from another team. I also ran bi-weekly check-ins focused on their first leadership decisions.
How did you handle the time?
I delegated the weekly 1:1s to the peer mentors after week two and only stepped in on escalations. This let me support four new managers without doubling my calendar load.
What was the retention or ramp result?
All four were still here at six months and two had already promoted a direct report.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Manager scaling to multiple new managers
Situation: Two new managers joined the org
Actions: Built 30-60-90 plan, assigned peer mentors, ran focused check-ins then delegated
Outcome: All four new managers retained at 6 months; two promoted a report
Quote: "I delegated the weekly 1:1s to the peer mentors after week two."
Follow-up: How did you handle the time? -> Leveraged peer mentors to create leverage
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at manager level. The candidate built a repeatable process and used peer mentors to create leverage instead of becoming the bottleneck. Focus on leadership decisions rather than task onboarding shows investment in people development. Six-month retention and early promotions provide concrete team outcome. Biggest strength: designed the system so support scaled beyond their direct time.

lowerTranscript.text: I met with the new manager weekly and answered their questions about our tools and processes.
Did you involve others or create any structure?
It was mostly me. I didn't have time to set up mentors.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Manager
Situation: New manager joined
Actions: Weekly 1:1s focused on tools and processes
Outcome: No leverage or broader involvement mentioned
Quote: "It was mostly me. I didn't have time to set up mentors."
Follow-up: Did you involve others or create any structure? -> No
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at manager level. The candidate relied on their own time without building team leverage or peer support. Onboarding stayed tactical and did not extend to leadership growth. No attempt to scale or involve the wider organization. Biggest gap: manager-level help should create repeatable mechanisms rather than remain one-to-one.

raiseTranscript.text: After a reorg added 40 new people across three regions, I defined a standardized onboarding curriculum with regional leads and tied it to our first-quarter OKRs. We measured time-to-first-commit and time-to-first-cross-region collab.
What trade-offs did you make?
We delayed two product launches by three weeks to free senior engineers for the first cohort. The data showed the investment paid off in Q2 velocity.
How did you sustain it?
After the first two cohorts I handed ownership to a program manager and only reviewed the metrics quarterly.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.
Role: Exec post-reorg
Situation: 40 new people across regions after reorg
Actions: Created standardized curriculum tied to OKRs, measured ramp metrics, traded short-term product work for long-term velocity
Outcome: Faster cross-region collaboration; Q2 velocity recovered
Quote: "We delayed two product launches by three weeks to free senior engineers for the first cohort."
Follow-up: What trade-offs did you make? -> Explicit product delay for onboarding investment
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at exec level. The candidate treated onboarding as an org-level system with measurable outcomes rather than ad-hoc help. They made a visible short-term business trade-off and handed off ownership once the process stabilized. Metrics on cross-region collaboration show strategic focus. Biggest strength: connected people development directly to business velocity with clear accountability transfer.

lowerTranscript.text: I sent a welcome note to the new execs and asked HR to handle the rest of onboarding.
Did you stay involved after the first week?
Not much. I assumed the teams would figure it out.

lowerNotes: Q: Describe a time you onboarded or helped a new team member get up to speed quickly.

Outcome: No follow-up or org-level measurement
Quote: "I assumed the teams would figure it out."

exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Teamwork & Collaboration at exec level. The candidate delegated onboarding entirely and showed no strategic ownership or measurement. No evidence of trade-off decisions or long-term thinking about org integration. The approach treats collaboration as a one-time courtesy rather than a leadership responsibility. Biggest gap: absence of leverage or accountability for cross-org ramp at executive scope.
